en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Ten,
Chapter on the Four Gates (Catudvāravagga)
6. The Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka:
“For seven days only, with a mind full of faith and seeking merit, did I practice the holy life under a teacher.”
Furthermore, this conduct of mine that I have practiced for more than fifty years—
I have carried it out even against my own will.
By this truth, may there be well-being!
May the poison be destroyed and Yaññadatta live!
Since I have never delighted in giving...
Having seen me as a guest at the time for lodging,
neither did they perceive any lack of affection in me,
nor did the learned recluses and brahmins.
Even though I gave it unwillingly,
by this truth may there be well-being;
let the poison be destroyed and Yajñadatta live!
“O dear one, there was a venomous snake of great power that bit you while wandering about;
because of my lack of affection for it today, [I am not angry].”
And there is no difference between you and your father;
by this truth, may there be well-being,
and may Yaññadatta, whose poison has been destroyed, live!
“Only those who are peaceful and self-controlled go forth into homelessness;
there are none other than the dark ones who are not subject to desire.
Dīpāyana, out of disgust for what?”
"You lead the holy life without desire.
"Having set out through faith, he has turned back again;
alas, this man is truly a fool, like a deaf-mute."
Disgusted by this doctrine,
I live the holy life against my will;
yet it is a state praised by the wise and esteemed by the virtuous.
"In this way, I become a doer of merit.
"You satisfy recluses, brahmins,
and travelers with food and drink, as well as those seeking alms;"
This house of yours is like a well, provided with food and drink; so why, out of loathing for what talk?...
[is it that you live as a recluse?]
“You give this gift without desire.
“My fathers and grandfathers were faithful, masters of giving, and generous;”
Following that minor rule of conduct,
may I not be the last of my lineage;
being loathsome toward this way of speaking, [may I not be so].
“I give this gift without desire.
“When I brought you, O fair-limbed one, from your kinsmen’s home as a young girl lacking in wisdom;”
And yet they did not know my lack of affection for them,
except for their pursuit of sensual pleasures; so,
in what way, O lady, could they have been dear to me?
“Such was the custom of cohabitation.
“It is far and distant, never existing here;
there is no such thing as ‘intermarriage’ within this family.”
Following that minor rule of conduct,
may I not be the last ill-famed woman in my family;
being disgusted by this way of life, [I shall strive].
“I am your unwilling foot-servant. “Mandavya,
that which I spoke which should not have been spoken—
forgive me for that today for the sake of my son.”
"There is no love for one's children here in this world nor in the next;
yet here he lives, our very own Yaññadatta.
Thus ends the sixth Jātaka, the Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka.
